common_name: Seminole Tangelo (Self-Fertile Duncan Grapefruit x Dancy Tangerine Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after frost danger passes, in full sun with excellent drainage. Unlike most other tangelos, self-fertile and does not require a second citrus cultivar nearby for pollination. Expect first significant fruiting 3-5 years after transplant.

directions: Seminole is a historic USDA-bred tangelo (Duncan grapefruit crossed with Dancy tangerine) valued for richly flavored, deep reddish-orange, very juicy flesh that many growers consider among the best-tasting of all tangelos, though the fruit is seedy and better suited to fresh eating and juicing than to easy peeling. Unlike Orlando and Minneola tangelos, Seminole is self-fertile and sets a full crop without a second citrus variety planted nearby. Fruit ripens later than most Gulf Coast citrus, typically hanging on the tree from late winter into spring and extending the home harvest season. As with other tangelos, cold hardiness is moderate rather than exceptional, so protect trees during hard freezes in zone 9a.
sources: University of California Riverside Givaudan Citrus Variety Collection

common_name: Southern Frost Navel Orange (UGA Cold-Hardy Seedless Navel Orange)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun on well-drained soil. Released by the University of Georgia specifically for the cool northern edge of the citrus belt and notably more freeze-tolerant than older navel oranges such as Washington Navel, but young trees still need frost cloth or other protection through their first winters.

directions: Southern Frost is a seedless navel orange released by the University of Georgia and bred by researcher Wayne Hanna for improved cold tolerance beyond standard navel oranges such as the Washington Navel already grown on the Gulf Coast. Fruit offers classic sweet navel orange eating quality and ripens in late fall. Growers and university trial reports describe the tree surviving temperatures as low as 15 degrees F with limited damage, making it one of the more freeze-tolerant sweet oranges available for zone 8b-9a dooryard planting, though hard freezes still call for protection. It was released alongside UGA's companion Frost series citrus, including Pink Frost grapefruit and Sweet Frost tangerine, as part of a coordinated effort to expand citrus options for Deep South gardeners.
sources: University of Georgia College of Agricultural and Environmental Sciences
University of Georgia Office of Research

common_name: Pink Frost Grapefruit (UGA Cold-Hardy Pink-Fleshed Grapefruit)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun with sharp drainage. Bred by the University of Georgia for reliable production farther north than standard grapefruit and reported hardy as far north as Tifton, Georgia, but young trees still need winter protection during hard freezes in zone 8b-9a.

directions: Pink Frost is a University of Georgia-released grapefruit bred by Wayne Hanna for reliable production at the cooler northern edge of the citrus range, and is reported hardy as far north as Tifton, Georgia, noticeably farther north than the standard grapefruit cultivars, which are among the least cold-tolerant citrus types. Fruit carries a deep pink blush on the rind over pink flesh, with a long harvest window running from late November through March. It fills a gap left by the grapefruit cultivars already in wide use (Marsh, Ruby Red, Star Ruby), which are generally recommended only for the mildest parts of zone 9b-10 rather than the cooler zone 8b-9a Gulf Coast. As with other grapefruit, protect young trees from hard freezes and expect several years before a substantial first crop.
sources: University of Georgia College of Agricultural and Environmental Sciences
University of Georgia Office of Research

common_name: Marathon Mandarin (Seedless UF/IFAS Daisy x Kishu Mandarin Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil. A modern University of Florida release bred mainly for fresh-market Florida growers, so it has typical mandarin cold hardiness rather than satsuma-level toughness; give young trees a sheltered site and frost protection in zone 9a.

directions: Marathon is a modern University of Florida mandarin release, a cross of Daisy mandarin and Seedless Kishu, valued for fruit that is completely seedless under any pollination conditions, easy to peel, and able to hold on the tree from October into January without becoming puffy or dry. It shows useful tolerance to citrus greening (HLB), an increasing concern for dooryard citrus. Cold hardiness is typical of standard mandarins rather than the exceptional range of satsuma or the UGA Frost series citrus, so plant in a warm microclimate and protect during hard freezes. Its parentage and extended on-tree storage distinguish it from the older Florida mandarin hybrids such as Sunburst, Robinson, Lee, and Nova already grown on the Gulf Coast.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Citrus Research and Education Center

common_name: Ten Degree Tangerine (Extreme-Cold-Hardy Clementine x Yuzu Hybrid, Clemyuz 2-2)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun with excellent drainage. Originated from Texas backyard citrus breeding rather than a university program, so it is sold mainly through specialty cold-hardy citrus nurseries rather than mainstream retailers; grown primarily for cold survival rather than dessert fruit quality.

directions: Ten Degree Tangerine (Clemyuz 2-2), a Clementine x Yuzu hybrid developed by Texas backyard citrus breeders, is grown mainly for extraordinary cold hardiness rather than dessert quality — the tart, lemonade-like flavored fruit is a bonus on a tree reported to have survived temperatures in the single digits Fahrenheit with only minor damage, notably hardier than satsuma, kumquat, or any other mandarin hybrid grown on the Gulf Coast. It has become a favorite among cold-hardy citrus hobbyists in south-central and southeast Texas, where winters occasionally drop below what satsuma or kumquat can reliably survive. Fruit ripens in late fall into early winter and, given its sharp, yuzu-influenced acidity, is more often used for juice, marmalade, or lemonade-style drinks than eaten fresh. Because it originated from hobbyist breeding rather than a university release, availability is limited mainly to specialty cold-hardy citrus nurseries.
